doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Acoustic bass and guitar versus amplified
summary: He values unplugged bass and guitar for their percussive energy and recalls Slam Stewart and Milt Hinton sweating through sets.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: York has a couple, two or three unplugged bass players. I mean really unplugged. They really play acoustic bass with gut strings. And it’s like fifty years ago. It’s wonderful because the souped up bass and acoustic guitar never really quite hit it off like totally acoustic. There’s also a factor of resistance in the guitar, when you have to work at it, and do this. You know when it’s amplified you have a little tiny pick and you have a light action, the strings lie close to the fingerboard, you don’t have to work, and you sort of go [scats]. And it’s sort of confidential. But when you really have to slug the damn thing, it gives it a percussive dimension that the other one doesn’t hand. And same thing with bass. I used to watch, it must have been Milt Hinton—I remember Slam Stewart with Benny Goodman and I remember the Calloway band around those years, ‘44, ‘45, so it must have been Milt and I remember it seemed to me that by the second number, you know they didn’t have any amps in those days, and by the second tune, the band jacket was already getting sweated through. But you felt that energy, that [scats] that you can’t quite get through an amp. Different.
They must have had some endurance.
You must have a lot of endurance too.
